当设备像书本一样半折叠时，系统会将弯曲处标记为不可用空间。文本和图像会自动向两侧退开；在诸如健身 App 的网格布局中，系统会自动在铰链两侧增加间距，确保交互方块避开折痕。
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/442-1.png!720
半折叠状态也被纳入了系统本身的使用逻辑。
将 iPhone Duo 以一定角度立在桌面上，设备可以直接进入重新设计的 StandBy 模式，把其中一侧屏幕变成时钟、照片或小组件显示区域。折叠在这里不再只是开与关两种状态，而是多出了一种可以长期停留的桌面形态。
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/443-1.png!720
与此同时，双屏互动也因此有了更多玩法。借助「场景配件（Scene Accessories）」API，应用可以让内外两块屏幕同时承担不同任务。
当用户在内屏进行拍摄或录像时，外屏可以显示独立的辅助内容，比如提词器，也可以向镜头另一侧的人展示提示画面或动画。苹果甚至专门提供了 CameraCaptureAccessory，让这类双屏拍摄体验成为标准开发能力。
https://images.ifanr.cn/wp-content/themes/ifanr-5.0-pc/static/images/zhixiaoyunqrcode.jpg
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/444-2.png!720
而机械铰链也成为了交互的一环。
苹果开放了实时读取铰链角度的 API（onHingeChange）。在官方演示中，弹奏虚拟吉他时，开合屏幕的角度变化被直接转化为「摇把变调」的输入信号。
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/445.png!720
Netflix、Slack 和 Zoom 等应用已经展示了针对 Duo 的定制界面，其中部分应用还会根据铰链开合角度实时调整控件位置。
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/446.png!720
而苹果真正值得观察的地方，也正在这里。它在折叠屏市场的硬件份额起步或许有限，却拥有推动整个 iOS 开发生态跟随新界面规范的能力。
在推出 Liquid Glass 时，苹果设计团队曾在接受媒体采访时透露，他们制作了大量真实玻璃样品，用于研究光线穿过玻璃时产生的折射、反射与聚焦效果。
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/447.png!720
时任人机交互设计副总裁 Alan Dye 对此解释道：「在苹果，我们始终坚信硬件与软件的深度融合，这使得人与技术之间的交互变得直观、美丽且令人愉悦。这是我们有史以来最广泛的一次软件设计更新。」
进入折叠屏时代后，Liquid Glass 的核心价值终于得以充分展现。
苹果今年 7 月份的时候，其实还公开了一项由人机交互设计团队主导的专利（US 2026/0219758 A1），或许能够帮助我们进一步理解未来交互设计的发展。
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/551.png!720
专利描述了一种「像果冻一样拉伸和压缩」的 UI 元素：系统不再依赖线性动画，而是根据手指滑动的具体角度与力度，实时计算 UI 模块的形变。
https://images.ifanr.cn/wp-content/themes/ifanr-5.0-pc/static/images/minappqrcode.jpg
或许是这种基于物理引擎的动态反馈，配合 A20 Pro 芯片（2 纳米制程）与双 16 核神经网络引擎的算力，让 iPhone Duo 整个界面的流转变得更加自然。
当然，如果智能手机行业有一个终极的工业设计愿景，那一定是 Jony Ive 曾反复描绘过的画面：「一台 iPhone，看起来像一片浑然天成的玻璃。」
2027 年适逢初代 iPhone 发布 20 周年，有传闻称，苹果推出一款颠覆外观的纪念产品。早期设想包括取消金属中框，让屏幕玻璃延伸至机身侧面，隐藏前置镜头，并以固态按键取代实体键，打造一体成型的全玻璃机身。
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/552.png!720
不过，据彭博社记者 Mark Gurman 最新的披露，受抗跌落性能和组装良率影响，量产版最终采用「玻璃与金属的折中」：正反两面为延伸至侧边的大面积曲面玻璃，中间仍保留金属边框，并非全玻璃机身。
在这个时间节点回头看 iPhone Duo 和 Liquid Glass，会发现硬件暂时还没能完全实现的无缝与纯粹，正由操作系统的底层机制，在数字空间里一点点补足。
https://s3.ifanr.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/553.png!720
芯片可以集成数百亿个晶体管，屏幕可以同时驱动两块面板，系统还要在每秒数千万次的计算中处理虚拟摄像头的朝向、保留区域的避让，以及铰链的夹角。
但系统设计最终要做的，是把这些越来越复杂的事情藏在背后，不让它们打扰用户。
二十年前，苹果希望手机看起来像一片玻璃。二十年后的今天，玻璃甚至不必保持固定的形状；只要用户在使用时，依然觉得这一切自然、顺畅，仿佛本来就该如此。
作者：莫崇宇

items.title: Kawakami Hiromi’s “Snack Futari”: One Last Drink Before I Go
items.summary: Internationally celebrated author Kawakami Hiromi creates her latest irresistible world in Snack Futari, which was recently published in Japan. A neighborhood
items.text:
Internationally celebrated author Kawakami Hiromi creates her latest irresistible world in Snack Futari, which was recently published in Japan. A neighborhood night spot is the setting for a buddy story between the two older women who run it, and a series of encounters with ghostly visitors who have unfinished business.

Kawakami Hiromi’s work deals with two types of fictional worlds. First are the allegorical works with thematic seriousness, like Under the Eye of the Big Bird, which was a finalist for the International Booker last year. Alongside these are books like Strange Weather in Tokyo, which charmed so many readers when it first appeared in the early 2000s and has recently gained an enthusiastic readership overseas. Much of the appeal of the books in this second category comes from the way they allow readers to immerse themselves in a beguiling fictional world and get to know the characters who live there. Kawakami’s latest novel to be published in Japan, Snack Futari, belongs firmly in the second category. I practically pumped the air when I picked up the book and felt its reassuring heft.

The setting of the story is a “snack” bar run by two women of indeterminate age.

Like most Japanese men of my generation, I have spent my fair share of time in “snacks.” A fixture of Japanese nightlife for decades, most snacks are small establishments where regulars make up the bulk of the clientele. Serving a range of staple drinks and simple food (often shōchū or whisky served from bottles behind the bar, each one marked with the name of a regular customer), each snack has its own atmosphere and mood reflecting the personality of the “mama-san.” The fictional snack of the novel is named Futari, which means “two people,” after the two women running it.

There are basically two types of snacks: glitzy bars in neon-drenched entertainment areas like Ginza and Shinjuku, and humbler establishments on the outskirts of town, where a small, illuminated sign might hang outside a building on an unassuming back street near the station. In my experience, the main difference between them is that whereas the bars in the bustling city centers often lean on sex appeal and the hint of flirtation, the ones in quieter areas stand or fall on the personality of the mama-san and the bar’s ability to offer a comforting environment where regulars can feel at home.

Snack Futari, perhaps unsurprisingly given that it is a bar imagined by Kawakami Hiromi, is definitely the latter type, though there are no details that would allow the reader to imagine where the bar might be located. The two women, Tsukasa and Itsuko, are both the “mama-san.” Although clearly no longer young, their precise age remains a mystery. In fact, we learn almost nothing about their background, or how they came to run the bar together. Almost the only thing we know about them is that they are single. This lack of information about the women’s pasts surely reflects a deliberate decision on the author’s part.

The novel consists of six episodes.

Tsukasa and Itsuko’s unpretentious neighborhood snack provides the setting for the stories that develop as the bar’s regulars visit the bar one after another at the end of their busy days. Structurally, the book is a series of linked short stories, all of them taking place within the confines of the eponymous snack. Each time, a new guest provides the focus of the narrative. One thing that makes the stories so enjoyable is the natural and convincing dialogue between the two owners.

Their conversations touch on the changing seasons and the insights that come with age, but really come to life when the two women discuss their regular customers and guests using their own distinctive turns of phrase. Before opening time each evening, they chat about the events of the night before. These conversations highlight Kawakami’s remarkable skill as a writer. The women’s remarks may occasionally be a little sharp, but there is no real cruelty or wish to put anyone down. Their words are imbued with the gentleness of age and seasoned with an understanding of human nature that is built on years of careful observation.

Indeed, as the author herself has remarked somewhere, the book resembles a kind of “buddy” story in which the two buddies happen to be elderly women. The obvious trust between them gives the stories a warm, poetic quality.

There is one other important characteristic of the novel.

The guests who appear in each episode are visitors from the world beyond. In other words, ghosts. These include the young uncle of one of the regulars, who died before he could fulfill his ambition to become a singer, and the mother of the owner of a local yakitori restaurant, who drops in from time to time. They are the ghosts of people who were forced to leave the world with important business still unresolved. In this respect, the stories can be compared to nō drama—specifically the world of mugen nō, in which a ghost appears to a traveling priest and narrates the disappointments or resentments that keep them from achieving peace, before performing a dance.

Of course, none of these stories resembles the tragic fate of the Heike courtiers who threw themselves into the sea after their defeat at Dannoura. For the most part, they are the kinds of everyday regrets that anyone might have, lingering attachments to people left behind, or simply the bewilderment of spirits unable to disappear. In many cases, these understated episodes would hardly constitute a story at all in the hands of a less gifted writer.

In Snack Futari, these ethereal spirits tell of their deepest feelings and then fade away, apparently purified. It is as if the bar functions as an exit, a departure terminal from which the dead return to the world beyond.

And at this point, I perhaps arrive at the answer to the question I had at the beginning.

Readers are told almost nothing about Tsukasa and Itsuko’s past—even their ages and physical appearance are left undescribed. The reason, it seems to me, is that the bar itself is not of this world. It is a dreamlike space where two elderly women live out their later years, and their attributes have been deliberately omitted for this reason. The bar is not only an ideal place for the regulars who spend their evenings there—it is also an ideal world for these women who live alone and have now reached old age.

For many years, snack bars suffered from a somewhat dowdy image. But recently, riding the wave of “retro” nostalgia for the Shōwa era (1926–89), I get the sense that even young salarymen are coming to appreciate the appeal of these bars. If so, this book may follow a similar trajectory to Strange Weather in Tokyo and become a long-term favorite.

For me, the time I spent reading the book made me feel as if I were perched on a stool in Snack Futari myself, listening to the inconsequential but reassuringly familiar everyday chatter of the two mama-sans. A place of comfort and ease, where the languid passage of time is captured perfectly in Kawakami’s simple but evocative prose.

But two hours is usually the right length of time to spend in a snack. Linger much longer and you may overindulge and say something you shouldn’t or pay the price the next day. And it costs money too.

Time to stand up from the stool and step outside to the tinkle of the cowbell over the door, back into the world of everyday reality.

Mama-san! I think it’s time for me to settle up and be on my way.

Ōkina tori ni sarawarenai yō is translated as Under the Eye of the Big Bird by Asa Yoneda.

Sensei no kaban is translated as Strange Weather in Tokyo by Allison Markin Powell.

items.title: Must-Try Spots For Noodle Lovers
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In
items.text:
Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”


Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.

1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway


This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.

2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam


Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.


At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.


3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan


This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.


You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.

4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana


Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.


5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia


In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.


Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)

6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan


Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.


Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!

7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain


This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.

8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York


Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.


While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.

9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand


Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.

10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore


For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.


After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

11. Lin Heung Tea House 📍 Hong Kong


Founded in the late 19th century, Lin Heung may just be Hong Kong’s oldest dim sum spot. It still does things the old-school way, too, with servers wheeling trolleys stacked high with bamboo steamers and calling out what dishes are up. Simply head over to the trolley and load up on what looks good to you, whether it’s rice noodle rolls, shrimp dumplings, pork ribs, or congee. The tea house can get quite crowded, so sharing a table with (or even befriending) fellow customers is simply a part of the experience.

12. Matsuka Seimen Noodle Factory 📍 Kurashiki, Japan


This gray shed functions mainly as a noodle factory, but during certain times of day, it changes gears to serve up freshly-cooked udon topped with eggs, scallions, and chili oil. Regulars swear by the kamatama: piping hot udon paired with nothing but a raw egg (cooked by the noodles) and a drizzle of soy sauce. Matsuka Seimen’s tiny kitchen also churns out a rich curry ramen made with fatty slivers of pork and soba noodles in a delicate green tea broth.


If you’re lucky, while you wait for your meal, you’ll witness the Matsuka family’s rather unusual noodle-kneading technique: A large tray of dough is covered in cloth and placed on the floor, where a family member walks all over it in special socks.

13. Bún Riêu Gánh 📍 Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam


On the busy streets of Ho Chi Minh City, Mrs. Mai Thi Lien serves up hefty ladles of simmering red broth from a massive pot on the sidewalk. Bún riêu, the noodle soup for which her restaurant is named, is made with rice vermicelli noodles and shrimp or pork mixed with crab paste, plus crispy tofu, huyet (coagulated pork blood), and herbs for garnishing. Mrs. Lien puts her own spin on the classic dish by pairing it with a tamarind fish sauce with sliced chili, giving it a distinctly southern Vietnamese flavor.

blocks.x: Humans have been slurping and savoring noodles for centuries, with the first recorded noodle dish recorded during China’s Eastern Han period (25–220 CE). In fact, noodles would go on to become inextricable from ancient Chinese culture, with a wheat-based version emerging as a staple of the Han dynasty. Centuries later, noodle-making would hit Europe, transforming the cuisines of Italy during the Middle Ages and Germany in the early 18th century. The English word “noodle” itself goes back to the 18th century, borrowed by the English from the German “nudel.”

Whatever you call them, one thing remains certain: Love of noodles transcends culture and country. Jacques Cousteau once said that the sea was “the great unifier ... man’s only hope,” but did he ever consider the power of a steaming bowl of ramen? For this delicious guide, we’ve noodled on the best of the best around the world—places where mind-bending broths and eccentric histories collide to create unforgettable dining experiences.
1. Hrimnir Ramen 📍 Oslo, Norway

This Oslo eatery puts a uniquely Norwegian spin on traditional Japanese ramen, using seasonal local ingredients found from the fjords to the mountains. Opened by Norwegian-American microbiologist David Quist in 2019, Hrimnir places a special focus on fermented ingredients, with jars of preserved lemons, pickled plums, and pear vinegar lining the walls. The noodles are handmade in house with emmer wheat or tokornkveite, a heritage grain that gives them a uniquely nutty flavor.
2. Phở Hàng Trống 📍 Hanoi, Vietnam

Hanoi is considered the birthplace of Vietnam’s staple noodle soup, phở, and in the living room of home chef Ms. Minh, you’ll find some of the very best in the country. She’s been selling phở in Hanoi for decades but was forced to take her business inside in 2017, when the city started cracking down on street vendors.

At plastic tables, visitors to Ms. Minh’s home can enjoy traditional, northern-style phở (which has lighter, clearer broth than that in the south). She serves her noodles with jars of homemade chili sauce and pickled garlic, plus the option of dipping Chinese youtiao doughnuts in the hot broth.
3. Inari Soba Mansei 📍 Tokyo, Japan

This small soba shop dates back to the early 1600s, where it appears in the legend of Takuzousu, a Buddhist monk and kitsune, or shapeshifting fox-spirit. It’s said that Takuzousu frequented this very shop, where the coins he paid with supposedly turned into leaves once their magic had worn off.

You’d never know the restaurant’s legendary history from the outside, but inside, you’ll find a bronze bell from the original Takuzousu shrine displayed in glass. The menu, too, pays tribute to the kitsune by serving aburaage, a fried tofu believed to be foxes’ favorite food.
4. Pekin Noodle Parlor 📍 Butte, Montana

Pekin Noodle Parlor is the oldest continuously-operating Chinese restaurant in the U.S., opened in 1911 in what was once a thriving Chinatown. Passed down through the same family for generations, Pekin radiates old-school charm: A flickering, neon sign welcomes visitors into a dimly-lit space with orange booths and individual eating cubicles, where food arrives by trolley. The parlor’s main draw is the Chinese-American classic, chop suey, but it also serves up a mean chow mein and chicken noodle soup.
5. Mie Lethek Garuda 📍 Srandakan, Indonesia

In this traditional factory, cows turn a huge mortar that grinds dried cassava and sweet potatoes into flour for mie lethek, the region’s signature noodle variety. Mie lethek translates to “ugly noodles,” an apt name for these squiggly gray creations. But what they lack in beauty, they make up for in flavor: sweeter than your average noodle, with a pleasant, chewy texture.

Yasir Feri, Mie Lethek Garuda’s owner, is the grandson of the noodle’s creators, a Yemeni/Chinese couple who first opened up shop in the 1940s. After the cows have created the flour, Feri and his factory workers mix and press the dough by hand, then leave the finished noodles to dry in the sun before bringing them to the market. (The cows are also given sweet grass in return for their hard work.)
6. Pure Love Diner Bar 📍 Taipei, Taiwan

Colorful neon signs welcome you into this ’80s-themed den of vice (and noodles), complete with red lighting, disco balls, and antique furniture. The diner is an homage to Taipei’s old-school karaoke bars, known as “grandpa shops” for their older—and often flirtatious—patrons, though without any of the original bars’ suspicious activity.

Here, it’s all about enjoying the kitschy ambiance and chowing down on Taiwanese classics like braised pork over rice, oyster soup, fried chicken, and deep-fried noodles in satay sauce. Plus, there’s still a karaoke machine in the corner!
7. Fideus de Vermar 📍 Binissalem, Spain

This small town of Binissalem celebrates its rich wine heritage with the annual Festa des Vermar, which includes (among plenty of wine-based activities) huge cauldrons of short noodles, slow-cooked meats, red wine, and aromatic spices. This traditional local paella, called fideus de vermar, serves all 1,400 of the town’s residents during the festival, turning the main square into a lively picnic spot.
8. Bamonte’s 📍 Brooklyn, New York

Founded by immigrants in 1900, this family institution holds the distinction of being Brooklyn’s oldest Italian restaurant. It was once a favorite meeting spot of the New York mafia, as well as a setting for the fictional New Jersey mob in “The Sopranos.” Other (more law-abiding) Italian-Americans of note, such as Robert De Niro and Frank Sinatra, have dined here, and the restaurant honors its many famous guests with framed photos on the walls.

While New York City has grown exceedingly expensive, Bamonte’s has kept its Italian classics surprisingly affordable, and crowd-pleasers like the rigatoni alla vodka and linguine with red clam sauce keep people coming back year after year.
9. Khanom Jeen Pa Mai 📍 Phuket Town, Thailand

Thin white rice noodles called khanom jeen are a staple throughout Thailand, where they’re served with various spicy curries, meats, and vegetables. At this unassuming eatery in Phuket Town, customization reaches new heights with a lineup of everything from crispy dried fish to pickled mustard greens to pineapple slices.
10. Hawker Chan Soya Sauce Chicken Rice & Noodle 📍 Singapore

For about $3, you can enjoy a Michelin-star meal at this Singapore noodle shop. Owner and chef Chan Hon Meng first opened Hawker Chan as a food-court stall, where it became famous with his “secret,” Cantonese-style chicken marinade. The flavorful braised meat is served over char siew noodles, rice, or hor fun noodles with stir-fried veggies and braised eggs.

After Meng took home a Michelin star in 2016 (which he at first assumed was a practical joke), he turned Hawker Chan into a full-scale restaurant right next to where his humble stall once stood. Since then, other locations have opened in Thailand, Kazakhstan, Laos, and Malaysia, with more still on the way.

items.text:
市场对美联储重启加息的担忧正在升温，令历史上一段颇具警示意味的周期重回投资者视野。花旗研究最新量化宏观策略报告显示，当前宏观环境与1988至1989年紧缩周期的相似程度明显上升，同时叠加中东局势再度升级与美国通胀压力重燃，跨资产配置逻辑正在悄然生变。


据追风交易台消息，花旗研究分析师Alex Saunders与Vinh Vo在9月11日发布的报告中指出，尽管其宏观模型（Regime Model）整体仍停留在"正常"（Normal）区间，但通胀动能趋强、经济意外指数温和回落，加之金融条件小幅收紧，令模型识别出的历史近似时期正在向1988至1989年靠拢。


值得注意的是，在1988年3月至1989年5/6月的这轮紧缩周期中，美联储共计加息16次。据天风证券孙彬彬团队统计，1988年3月，美联储为防止再次进入高通胀，选择提前紧缩。1988年3月30日，FOMC会议将联邦基金利率上调25bp至6.75%，此后共计加息16次，最终联邦基金利率目标上调至9.8125%，共计加息331.25bp。


1980年代末时期的典型特征是：经济维持韧性、通胀压力逐步积累，最终促使美联储持续加息，随后经济活动放缓，政策才转向宽松。报告同时将1976至1977年、1996至1997年及2013至2014年列为其他参照历史区间。

在资产配置层面，上述宏观背景驱使模型进一步增持风险资产，并确立了鲜明的结构性偏好：做多新兴市场与美国股票、做多日本和英国久期，同时将美国投资级信用债的空头维持在最大权重，以能源为核心做多大宗商品，并转向偏好美元。

1988至1989年紧缩周期重回视野

花旗研究的历史近似分析显示，1988至1989年在本月明显变得更为突出。报告描述，这一时期呈现出经济韧性与通胀压力并存的组合——正是这一组合促使美联储在1988年持续收紧货币政策，直至次年经济活动放缓后才转向降息。


这与当前宏观状态高度契合。模型显示，经济增长指标温和改善，PMI z分数平均值仍处于强劲水平，经济意外指数虽略有回落，但绝对水平依然积极；与此同时，通胀动能在过去一个月有所回升，金融条件小幅收紧，整体仍处于长期均值以下约0.55个标准差。报告将当前宏观状态定性为"经济过热"症状——增长与通胀指标均略高于长期均值，但尚未触发模型切换。


报告同时保留了其他三个历史参照区间：1976至1977年（前沃尔克时代，通胀下行与宽松金融条件并存，初期支撑股市，但随后通胀和政策利率大幅上升）；1996至1997年（互联网扩张初期）；以及2013至2014年（美联储缩减购债预期推动美国利率重定价）。值得注意的是，去年关税冲击在最新模型中已不再构成有意义的近似历史参照，花旗研究认为这反映出跨资产长期波动率仍处于相对低位。

模型坚守"正常"区间，股票仓位进一步提升


“新美联储通讯社”Nick Timiraos最新撰文称，投资者已基本认定美联储下周将进行三年来首次加息，更难的问题是之后会怎样。自1990年代以来，美联储仅有一次“一次性”加息。

尽管市场对加息的担忧升温，花旗研究的K近邻（KNN）模型仍维持在"正常"区间，并未向"金融条件收紧"区间切换。报告指出，在本月更新后，模型将股票超配比例从2.8%进一步上调至4.0%，债券与大宗商品维持正配置（但有所削减），信用债空头仓位则保持不变。


报告同时提示了潜在的下行路径：若能源冲击以持续性主题延续——无论是补库需求驱动还是供应流中断——金融条件收紧与信用利差走阔或将成为通往滞胀情景的传导链条。


在不同模型下的历史夏普比率表现方面，"正常"区间的资产表现与无条件历史均值相近，债券属性略占优势，而美国股票相对其他地区具有一定优势。

跨资产配置：能源领衔，美元取代日元成偏好货币

在具体资产配置上，花旗研究模型呈现出高度差异化的结构。股票方面，新兴市场获得最高配置，美国股票保持小幅多头，欧洲、日本和英国股票则被做空。


利率方面，债券整体超配3.7%，日本和英国久期获最大多头配置，美国国债则被最大化做空，欧洲债券小幅做空。这一配置逻辑部分与欧洲央行加息后的鹰派前瞻指引及法国国债风险溢价上升有关。


大宗商品方面，能源是当前最强预期表现资产，模型集中超配能源，辅以小幅基本金属多头和贵金属小幅空头。报告指出，能源在相对持有成本（carry）维度上的优势远超其他商品子类，而基本金属和贵金属的carry则明显为负。


在外汇方面，报告指出市场对日元的热情已明显消退，英镑、日元和欧元对美元的预期夏普比率均为负值，使美元成为当前首选货币。这一转变部分源于美国财政部长贝森特在日本干预问题上的表态，以及市场对日本央行（BoJ）更早、更快收紧政策的预期推动日元阶段性升值后的动能减弱。


趋势跟踪策略年初至今维持正收益，系统性策略表现分化

从量化策略表现来看，趋势跟踪策略在过去一个月录得正收益，大宗商品和债券的强劲涨幅足以覆盖股票的损失以及基本持平的外汇贡献。值得关注的是，债券趋势跟踪策略在本月的收益完全逆转了此前的年初至今负收益，推动综合策略整体转正。大宗商品仍是年初至今最大贡献来源，股票则表现最弱。


套息（carry）策略过去一个月综合表现为正，商品和债券贡献了主要收益，外汇和股票套息则承压。报告同时指出，商品价值策略年初至今持续领涨，但股票和债券价值策略仍为负收益，且随着中东局势再度升级推动市场重新定价通胀与政策风险，债券价值策略进一步走弱。


在CTA定位方面，信用债维持最大多头，股票和大宗商品多头被削减至接近中性。

在资产配置层面，上述宏观背景驱使模型进一步增持风险资产，并确立了鲜明的结构性偏好：做多新兴市场与美国股票、做多日本和英国久期，同时将美国投资级信用债的空头维持在最大权重，以能源为核心做多大宗商品，并转向偏好美元。
1988至1989年紧缩周期重回视野
花旗研究的历史近似分析显示，1988至1989年在本月明显变得更为突出。报告描述，这一时期呈现出经济韧性与通胀压力并存的组合——正是这一组合促使美联储在1988年持续收紧货币政策，直至次年经济活动放缓后才转向降息。
这与当前宏观状态高度契合。模型显示，经济增长指标温和改善，PMI z分数平均值仍处于强劲水平，经济意外指数虽略有回落，但绝对水平依然积极；与此同时，通胀动能在过去一个月有所回升，金融条件小幅收紧，整体仍处于长期均值以下约0.55个标准差。报告将当前宏观状态定性为"经济过热"症状——增长与通胀指标均略高于长期均值，但尚未触发模型切换。
报告同时保留了其他三个历史参照区间：1976至1977年（前沃尔克时代，通胀下行与宽松金融条件并存，初期支撑股市，但随后通胀和政策利率大幅上升）；1996至1997年（互联网扩张初期）；以及2013至2014年（美联储缩减购债预期推动美国利率重定价）。值得注意的是，去年关税冲击在最新模型中已不再构成有意义的近似历史参照，花旗研究认为这反映出跨资产长期波动率仍处于相对低位。
模型坚守"正常"区间，股票仓位进一步提升
“新美联储通讯社”Nick Timiraos最新撰文称，投资者已基本认定美联储下周将进行三年来首次加息，更难的问题是之后会怎样。自1990年代以来，美联储仅有一次“一次性”加息。
尽管市场对加息的担忧升温，花旗研究的K近邻（KNN）模型仍维持在"正常"区间，并未向"金融条件收紧"区间切换。报告指出，在本月更新后，模型将股票超配比例从2.8%进一步上调至4.0%，债券与大宗商品维持正配置（但有所削减），信用债空头仓位则保持不变。
报告同时提示了潜在的下行路径：若能源冲击以持续性主题延续——无论是补库需求驱动还是供应流中断——金融条件收紧与信用利差走阔或将成为通往滞胀情景的传导链条。
在不同模型下的历史夏普比率表现方面，"正常"区间的资产表现与无条件历史均值相近，债券属性略占优势，而美国股票相对其他地区具有一定优势。
跨资产配置：能源领衔，美元取代日元成偏好货币
在具体资产配置上，花旗研究模型呈现出高度差异化的结构。股票方面，新兴市场获得最高配置，美国股票保持小幅多头，欧洲、日本和英国股票则被做空。
利率方面，债券整体超配3.7%，日本和英国久期获最大多头配置，美国国债则被最大化做空，欧洲债券小幅做空。这一配置逻辑部分与欧洲央行加息后的鹰派前瞻指引及法国国债风险溢价上升有关。
大宗商品方面，能源是当前最强预期表现资产，模型集中超配能源，辅以小幅基本金属多头和贵金属小幅空头。报告指出，能源在相对持有成本（carry）维度上的优势远超其他商品子类，而基本金属和贵金属的carry则明显为负。
在外汇方面，报告指出市场对日元的热情已明显消退，英镑、日元和欧元对美元的预期夏普比率均为负值，使美元成为当前首选货币。这一转变部分源于美国财政部长贝森特在日本干预问题上的表态，以及市场对日本央行（BoJ）更早、更快收紧政策的预期推动日元阶段性升值后的动能减弱。
趋势跟踪策略年初至今维持正收益，系统性策略表现分化
从量化策略表现来看，趋势跟踪策略在过去一个月录得正收益，大宗商品和债券的强劲涨幅足以覆盖股票的损失以及基本持平的外汇贡献。值得关注的是，债券趋势跟踪策略在本月的收益完全逆转了此前的年初至今负收益，推动综合策略整体转正。大宗商品仍是年初至今最大贡献来源，股票则表现最弱。
套息（carry）策略过去一个月综合表现为正，商品和债券贡献了主要收益，外汇和股票套息则承压。报告同时指出，商品价值策略年初至今持续领涨，但股票和债券价值策略仍为负收益，且随着中东局势再度升级推动市场重新定价通胀与政策风险，债券价值策略进一步走弱。
在CTA定位方面，信用债维持最大多头，股票和大宗商品多头被削减至接近中性。
以上精彩内容来自追风交易台。

items.title: America’s oldest restaurant is a 350-year-old historic tavern just 40 minutes from NYC — once famously known as ‘America’s spy prison’
items.author: Natalia Alvarez
items.summary: Tucked away in the tiny town of Tappan, New York, sits a dining destination older than the United States itself. The ’76 House isn’t just a pitstop for
items.text:
Tucked away in the tiny town of Tappan, New York, sits a dining destination older than the United States itself. The ’76 House isn’t just a pitstop for incredible comfort food—it is widely considered America’s oldest restaurant.


Built in 1668, this Hudson Valley gem has been pouring pints for over three centuries. It offers New Yorkers the ultimate historical day trip just 40 minutes from Manhattan.


A revolutionary history


Source / The 76 House
During the height of the Revolutionary War, the tavern served as a safe haven for weary patriots and military leaders. In fact, George Washington and his chief provisioner Samuel Fraunces famously dined within these very walls.


But its most dramatic claim to fame happened in 1780. The ’76 House acted as the makeshift prison for Major John André, the British spy who conspired with infamous traitor Benedict Arnold to surrender West Point.


André’s capture and imprisonment here shifted the entire course of the war, permanently earning the tavern its legendary nickname: ‘America’s spy prison’.

@history.unlimited


The Old ’76 House has been a haven for many a weary traveler for more than two hundred years. This great tavern has accommodated on various occasions, every General of the west wing of the Continental Army including Commander-in-Chief General George Washington who, with his chief provisioner Samuel Fraunces, dined in the comfortable atmosphere of The Old ’76 House during the American Revolutionary War. A house that sat on the spot of the existing building was originally built by Dutch settlers and operated as a stop for fur traders traveling north or south along the Hudson River. No further mentioning of the structure exists in documents however from around 1686 to 1705. The earliest confirmed dates concerning any structure on or near the current site involve one Antie Myers, a widow, who was licensed in 1705 to sell drink, “as per her recognizance,” in her house in the immediate neighborhood of today’s ’76 House. After her death around 1721 her home was purchased by Yoast Mabie, a brother of Casparus. The house was demolished in 1835. In 1753, Casparus Mabie bought a piece of land from Cornelis Myers, Antie’s son. The following year he built a house on this lot on what was to become Main Street in Tappan. He included space for a tavern, probably no more than a few tables and benches in a corner of the front room. Two years later, in 1756, court records indicate that the “Supervisors for the County of Orange [met] at the House of Casparus Maybe, in Orange Town October the 5th Anno Domine 1756.” These documents describe meetings of the Board of Supervisors over the years and provide details of the food and ale they consumed and the business they conducted. Consequently, the sign lists “1755” as the founding date for the current tavern. Of the structure that was built in 1668, only the foundation remains. The house remains a fixture as a place of great significance in American history. It is on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places. 76House.com, Britannica, Rockland County Historical Society, Tappan Historical District Association, U.S. National Register of Historic Places, Wikipedia #history #americanrevolutionarywar #americanrevolution #newyorkhistory #revolutionarywar #tappanny #tavern #fyp


♬ original sound – History Unlimited


What’s on the menu today


Source / The 76 House
Lovingly restored by the Norden family, the space feels like stepping back in time. You can still dine surrounded by centuries-old timber beams and four glowing fireplaces.


The menu elevates classic American pub fare into an incredible culinary experience. Today’s visitors can feast on:

The famous Onion Soup Lafayette, served en crock and au gratin.


Chicken Pot Pie: roasted Amish chicken and garden vegetables within a creamy velouté, served in a tender puff pastry shell.


Thanksgiving Spring Roll: Roasted turkey, cornbread stuffing, cranberry aioli.

On weekends, the tavern comes alive with local live music, keeping the centuries-old tradition of communal gathering going strong.

items.title: An East Village Dumpling Spot Shuts Down
items.summary:
The veggie dumplings at Mimi Cheng’s. | Mimi Cheng’s

This is Eater’s guide to all the New York City restaurants, bars, and cafes that closed in September
items.text:
The veggie dumplings at Mimi Cheng’s. | Mimi Cheng’s

This is Eater’s guide to all the New York City restaurants, bars, and cafes that closed in September 2026. This list will be updated weekly (see: August, July, June, May, April, March, February, January), serving as a round-up of the dining and drinking places that have shuttered around the city. If a restaurant or bar has closed in your neighborhood, let us know at ny@eater.com.

September 4

Spotlight

East Village: Mimi Cheng’s serves its last dine-in dumpling on Friday, September 11, noting the lease was up at this sole standalone location. “While closing this storefront will be sentimental, it means we get to pour everything into what’s next,” per a closing statement. Over its 12-year run, the tiny shop evolved into a nationwide business found in Whole Foods’ freezer aisles, and the plan is to continue to scale operations apart from its physical digs. The team is currently fielding interest from bars, restaurants, hotels, events, arenas, and other retail stores looking to sell its dumplings. A menu collab with Brooklyn’s Pizza Loves Emily featuring dry-aged beef-stuffed dumplings marked its final days of sit-down service in September. 179 Second Avenue, between East 11th and 12th streets

And the rest…

Bed-Stuy: Brooklyn’s blue-toned coffee shop, the Bureau, quietly shut down this week, notes Bed-Stuy Stoop, saying the building was repossessed by the city and handed back to the landlord. Chef Ayo Balogun also owns popular places like Dept of Culture and Radio Kwara in the same Brooklyn neighborhood. The Bureau went through several iterations under the same owners over its 13-year run, first as a basic cafe called Civil Service (which had to close after a car crashed into its window in 2018). It later reopened as Council Cafe before ultimately becoming the Bureau three years ago. 279 Nostrand Avenue, at Clifton Place

Brooklyn Heights: After 30 years in Brooklyn, family-run grocer All in One Deli Mart, fondly known as Peas N’ Pickles, closed its doors for good. Owner Minki Lee previously cited a spike in property taxes and rent as the cause for the closure. The neighborhood grocer also offered a vast prepared foods section full of subs, soups, and sushi. 79 Henry Street, at Pineapple Walk

Williamsburg: Boil n Bite, Brooklyn’s seafood boil destination loaded up with clams, calamari, crab, fish and chips, surf-and-turf options, and more, announced its closure on Instagram on Thursday, August 10. 148 N. Seventh Street, between Berry Street and Bedford Avenue

September 4

Spotlight

East Village: Double Zero, the vegan pizza and wine bar from celebrity vegan chef and raw food advocate Matthew Kenney, permanently closed this week after 12 years. “We have made the difficult decision that continuing Double Zero is no longer financially sustainable,” per signage on the door flagged by EV Grieve, citing rising food and operating costs, the “realities of our lease,” and an overall slowdown in demand for vegan dining.

Double Zero specialized in personal wood-fired pies topped with shiitake bacon and nut-based cheeses like cashew mozzarella to go along with sustainable wines. Back in 2018, Kenney announced plans to bring the restaurant to Philadelphia, plus other places like Brooklyn, Boston, and Los Angeles; ultimately, however, those locations never materialized. The James Beard-nominated chef and cookbook author previously opened several meat- and dairy-free restaurants across the globe.

The brand has gone through several changes recently. In early 2025, Double Zero and Bar Verde merged into one restaurant called PlantMade, which offered a combination menu of vegan pizzas and Mexican fare. Earlier this year, Kenney rejoined the team as consulting chef and flipped Double Zero back to its original form and name in the space next door to the Second Avenue original. (Its very first name, 00 + Co., confused customers and was quickly changed.) 65 Second Avenue, at Fourth Street

And the rest…

Union Square: Max Brenner, the whimsical chocolatier that commanded long lines in its early days, closed on Saturday, August 29, after 20 years of catering to the touristy Times Square crowd. Built as a restaurant, chocolate retailer, and interactive dessert bar all in one, Max Brenner served crepes, choctails, pizza topped with chocolate chunks, sweet waffles, and decadent fondue. A Reddit user who flagged the closure noted a post-COVID slump in sales under new ownership. 841 Broadway, between East 13th and 14th streets

West Village: Korean chef Jihan Lee’s TBD Gimbap held its last week of service in late August. TBD, as its name suggested, was technically always meant to be a pop-up (Lee previously told Eater it’d be open until at least May; it ended up lasting six months). The pint-sized takeout strictly specialized in seaweed-wrapped gimbap like his mom used to make, rolled to order and filled with beef bulgogi, spicy carrots, and spicy pork. “This isn’t goodbye. It’s just this chapter closing so the next one can start,” writes Lee in a closing statement, adding that “more gimbap is coming.” The Masa alum is also a partner at next-door Japanese hand roll bar Nami Nori since 2019, which has since expanded to New Jersey, Florida, and Virginia. 31 Carmine Street, near Bleecker Street

It’s just this chapter closing so the next one can start,” writes Lee in a closing statement, adding that “more gimbap is coming.” The Masa alum is also a partner at next-door Japanese hand roll bar Nami Nori since 2019, which has since expanded to New Jersey, Florida, and Virginia. 31 Carmine Street, near Bleecker Street

The scallop dish at Amphora. | Alex Staniloff

This is Eater’s guide to all the new restaurants, bars, and cafes that have opened this week in September 2026. Throughout the month, we’ll update the list weekly (see: August, July, June, May, April, March, February, January). When we’ve been to a place, we will then include a few openings on our heatmaps (Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, cocktail bars) to let you know the ones we like. If there’s an opening in your neighborhood that we’ve missed, let us know at ny@eater.com.

September 9

Spotlight

Flatiron: Amphora, a tasting room boasting one of the city’s biggest wine collections, opens on Wednesday, September 9, in the long-closed home of oenophile favorite Veritas. Executive chef Jack Logue (formerly of now-closed the Lambs Club and Betony) sends out three- and four-course menus, with a la carte options at the bar. Named for the ancient vessel used to transport wine across civilizations, Amphora is stocked with over 2,500 labels — making it one of NYC’s largest wine cellars. Wine director Chris Miller, a fellow Lambs Club alum, spotlights regions like Burgundy, Northern Rhone, Piedmont, and Champagne from top producers that include Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, Coche-Dury, Raveneau, and Rousseau. 43 E. 20th Street, at Rutherford Place

And the rest…

Bed-Stuy: Mexican restaurant Olmo doubles down on the block with a collaborative new all-day taqueria and cafe called Peral. The team-up with Mexico City cafe and bar Cicatriz opened right next door to Olmo on Wednesday, September 2. Peral’s menu leans more casual than Olmo (see: tacos, many of which are guisados) with an affinity towards vegetarian and vegan options. 105 Saratoga Avenue, near Decatur Street

Chelsea: Vegan cinnamon roll bar Cinnaholic opened its first physical location in Chelsea over Labor Day weekend, inviting customers to jazz up gooey rolls with customizable toppings like fresh fruit, cookie dough, and chocolate drizzle. Coffee Project New York supplies the caffeine on-site. 228 Eighth Avenue, at West 22nd Street

Crown Heights: Brooklyn’s acclaimed Haitian patty pop-up Bon Pâtés debuted its first physical storefront over Labor Day weekend. Walk-up hours for its freshly baked patties are Thursday to Sunday from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., and catering and nationwide shipping are also still available. 637 Nostrand Avenue, at St Marks Avenue

Greenpoint: The owners of Wasabi, the Brooklyn sushi staple that closed this summer after a 26-year run, are back in the game with a new Japanese spot down the street. Ayune, which opened on Monday, September 7, specializes in hand rolls filled with the likes of tuna, salmon, shiitake mushrooms, or Japanese pumpkin, available in sets of three, four, five, or six ($19 to $38). Ayune takes over the former home of Botbar — a robot-run cafe with vegan food from Wasabi. At Ayune, expect a pared-down selection of Wasabi’s familiar favorites, owners Robby and Cristin Wijaya tell Greenpointers. While a beer and wine license awaits, Ayune serves nonalcoholic options like spicy mango coolers, yuzu shiso fizzes, lemonade, and teas. 664 Manhattan Avenue, between Norman and Nassau avenues

Long Island City: At Rewind — a 9,000-square-foot underground restaurant, cocktail bar, and karaoke lounge, which debuted on Wednesday, September 9 — diners enter by pressing a “rewind” button on an ’80s-style boombox that opens onto the bar. That’s where beverage director Ken Chen, formerly of Taipei’s Indulge Experimental Bistro, builds cocktails on tea, the Chinese zodiac, and the five elements. Partner Alexander Lee’s menu includes truffle mushroom congee, Taiwanese fried chicken, and wagyu donburi. Beyond the restaurant are eight private karaoke rooms inspired by Hong Kong cinema, vintage recording studios, and other retro references. Rewind will also host a monthly guest bartender series featuring bartenders from New York spots like Stone & Soil, Yawning Cobra, and Red Sorghum. Rewind is co-founded by AYS Hospitality (behind NYC’s Mr. Moto’s collection of restaurants). 45-57 Davis Street, between Jackson and Skillman avenues

Lower East Side: Billed as “NYC’s most interesting sandwich shop,” ironically named Boring Sandwich opened inside a bodega on Saturday, September 5, with a globe-trotting assortment of gourmet sandwiches from chef Michael Brafman. The Shok-Shoe-Ka piles North African stewed tomato on an Aleppo bagel from Curly’s in Queens; a towering steak-and-egg Chivito pays homage to Uruguay’s national dish; and a New Orleans-styled muffuletta (a pressed Italian hero) also makes an appearance in the hidden dining destination that stays open until 10 p.m. Other orders include a tempura roll sandwich; chopped cheese riff; and another with Spam, tomato, crispy onion, and mala sauce. 97 Stanton Street, between Orchard and Ludlow streets

Soho: A new shop dedicated to single-source cacao with a bakery and cafe components, ÓOL, opened on Wednesday, September 9. Founder Ilana Gutierrez, who is from Mexico City, is showcasing single-origin cacao from Ecuador, Colombia, and Belize; it’s used for drinks with milks and/or water, along with spiced syrups like chile or ginger. ÓOL is partnering with NYC chain Breads Bakery for pastries made with that cacao, like a cacao swirl, cacao chop cookie, and a cacao croissant. In the near future, the two-story space will host tastings and workshops. 178 Spring Street, near Thomson Street

Tribeca: Keith McNally’s son, George, opened his first restaurant, Faux, on Thursday, September 3. McNally (the son) knows the restaurant life well, having worked at his father’s spots like Balthazar and the D.C. location of Minetta Tavern. Faux’s chef Kristina Ramos (who worked at Minetta in D.C.) is cooking up a coastal French menu, with highlights including broiled oysters and steak frites. The ground-floor restaurant includes a downstairs bar, Prevz, with late-night food and a bouncer. Book restaurant reservations on OpenTable. 277 Church Street, between White and Franklin streets

Tribeca: Evento, the nearly decade-old Italian hospitality company known for its cooking classes, culinary workshops, pasta-making dance parties, and big-ticket corporate events from Italian-born chef Andrea Belfiore and co-founder Sam Akiba, opened its first permanent home on Friday, September 4. The Manhattan flagship, housed inside the historic three-story Bogardus Mansion, is split up into three sections: a ground-floor cooking studio fit for pizza and pasta parties and workshops; a private dining room on the second floor dressed in Italian decor; and a forthcoming restaurant on the lower level. 75 Murray Street, between West Broadway and Greenwich Street

Upper East Side: Soba noodle house Kuriya, from the neighborhood team behind Japanese rice bowl restaurant Suki Desu, debuted on Sunday, September 6. Noodles presented on a tatami mat can be dipped in gyudon or topped with raw seafood, notes Infatuation. 219 E. 85th Street, between Second and Third avenues

Upper East Side: Bronx-born New York native, chef Lana Lagomarsini — a semifinalist on Top Chef season 22 and Gramercy Tavern alum — opens a supper clubby tasting menu spot centered on the Black culinary diaspora, on Wednesday, September 9. Creola, named after her grandmother, prepares courses like potlikker consomme (a nod to her grandmother’s collard greens) and oxtail pate en croute that riffs on the French pastry-wrapped meat dish. The $125 tasting menu is joined by $65 wine pairings. 1261 Park Avenue, between East 97th and 98th streets

Upper West Side: Derek Wu, the former manager of Lower East Side Chinese restaurant Wu’s Wonton King, heads across Central Park with the debut of Wu’s Dynasty on Thursday, September 3. As first reported by West Side Rag, the Cantonese newcomer is huge — it takes up 8,000 square feet — and does dim sum daily (with roving carts rolling around from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.). The parade of plates includes pan-fried Chinese chive and shrimp dumplings, pan-fried noodles with beef, cheong fun (steamed rice rolls), and custard lava buns. Live seafood and huge crustaceans like king crab greet customers upon entry inside tanks, and there’s Beijing duck, too. A bar serves cocktails, whiskeys, and wines. Hours run until 10 p.m. daily. 208 West 70th Street, between West End and Amsterdam avenues

Washington Heights: Eventually hoping to also be a bistro and bar, the ambitious new Boogie Lab opens as just an artisan bakery stocked with to-go loaves to start. “But this is just step one,” notes the team. Coming soon: food, drinks, music, and “an inviting space that shifts its rhythm from day to night.” 4015 Broadway, at West 169th Street

September 2

Spotlight

Midtown: After a revamp, iDen’s Beijing Duck House reopened on Tuesday, September 1, in its former La Grenouille space. The updated high-end duck restaurant originally opened in NYC last year, after its sibling location in Vancouver which had opened six years ago. The chef, Matt Chen, had run the kitchen of Le Palais in Taipei — apparently the first restaurant in Taiwan to receive three Michelin stars — retooled the menu, now featuring a $200 tasting menu as well as a la carte options like a duck-egg yolk roll; surf clam and okra salad; venison with Sichuan-pickled vegetables; and the Beijing duck, which starts at $128. 3 E. 52nd Street, between Fifth and Madison avenues

And the rest…

Chelsea: Showy clubstaurant STK Steakhouse has expanded its presence in the city, opening a spacious second location in Chelsea in mid-August. Diners — the space can fit 200 of them — will find the same steaks, seafood, cocktails, and “DJ-driven dining” (per a press release) that have kept the Midtown location going for nearly two decades. The restaurant will launch a seasonal pumpkin-focused menu beginning Wednesday, September 9, which includes offerings such as crab-stuffed shrimp in pumpkin cream sauce and pumpkin spice margaritas. The space was previously home to another flashy den of meat: Salt Bae’s Nusr-Et Steakhouse, which closed in 2024. 412 W. 15th Street, between Ninth and Tenth avenues

Chinatown: The team behind Essex Street’s old-timey photo booth Retrography unveiled a secret new cafe called Behind The Booth in the back on Wednesday, August 26. The slim-and-stylish setup specializes in an “unexpected” wine list and “ice cream you wouldn’t have ordered anywhere else,” per an opening message. 15 Essex Street, between Canal and Hester streets

Greenpoint: Acclaimed Lone Star pitmasters Jonny White and Chuck Charnichart brought Brooklyn a legit Texas barbecue joint on Sunday, August 30, with the opening of Kirbee’s. Their respective restaurants — Goldee’s in Fort Worth and Barbs B Q in Lockhart — are some of the best barbecue joints in the country over the last several years, with Michelin nods, James Beard nominations, and more. Charnichart’s barbecue plate features her South Texan and Mexican takes on barbecue: pork ribs with lime zest, brisket with Mexican spices, charro beans, and the iconic green spaghetti. White’s is more modern, with brisket, ribs, turkey, potato salad, and coleslaw. Each will include pickles and bread. Kirbee’s works like a true Texas barbecue: People line up outside the black-and-red storefront and place their orders at the first window; their orders will be cut up and plated inside; and then they’ll pick up their trays at the second window; after which they can either find a table in the 24-seat dining room. 55 McGuinness Boulevard South, between Engert Avenue and Newton Street

Greenpoint: Cozy corner coffee shop Loco Cafe opened in the small 500-square-foot space that was previously home to short-lived Viva La Pizza and Pizza Prince on Saturday, August 29, and the minimalist replacement inside has a winking cup of Joe logo. 626 Manhattan Avenue, at Nassau Avenue

Greenwich Village: The swanky martini destination Chateau Royale has been flipped into the more neighborhood-y Floradora, which opened on Thursday, August 27. The new menu features snacks such as mozzarella sticks and pigs in a blanket, alongside French dip sandwiches, burgers, disco fries, chicken paillard, two-layer oxtail lasagna, and more. (The drinks menu, meanwhile, leans into tiny ’tinis and other “sorta-’tinis.”) As owners Cody Pruitt and Jacob Cohen have told Eater NY, the flip was motivated by a desire to make the restaurant “more accessible, price-wise, as well as cuisine-wise, and vibe-wise, so we can see our neighbors more often;” diners at Chateau Royale tended to order the burger over the pricier Dover sole. It’s the second flip this summer for Pruitt and Cohen, who transitioned Libertine in the West Village into the “seafood tavern” Capitaine in June. 205 Thompson Street, at Bleecker Street

Upper East Side: Bright-orange Italian restaurant and pizzeria La Collina opened on Tuesday, August 18, for lunch, dinner, and brunch. Red and white pies join a namesake mozzarella salad and mains like Mediterranean sea bass with celery root puree or sirloin steak surrounded by roasted potatoes, plus a coconut Negroni or limoncello elixirs at the bar. A $34 two-course lunch option during the week features thinly sliced eggplant followed by tonnarelli cacio e pepe or tagliatelle Bolognese. 1431 First Avenue, at East 74th Street

West Village: NYC’s summer of Thai food continues on Wednesday, September 2, with the debut of Hommali from a trio of friends from Bangkok. The contemporary new spot rooted in Thailand’s beloved jasmine rice also offers a tom yum seafood cocktail; dry-aged duck breast served with fermented chile sauce; and penang curry with beef cheeks. A bar with a knack for fermentation and infusions slings drinks like the Tomato — a take on the michelada and a spritz, which includes a Singaporean rice wine made with jasmine and sticky rice. 28 Seventh Avenue South, near Leroy Street

Williamsburg: Small Change, a new bar from the team behind the Last Resort in the East Village and One Trick Pony in the West Village, opened in June in the former location of Lady Jay’s (which occupied the space for almost 15 years). The large backyard remains ready for group hangs, now with an awning of plants. Happy hour runs from 4 to 7 p.m., featuring draft beers and well drinks for $5, plus other drink specials. The beer-and-shot combo runs $8 all day. 633 Grand Street, near Leonard Street

Williamsburg: Finally, Ugly Baby has returned, having opened its new location on Thursday, August 27, in the corner spot that once housed Emmy Square Pizza. The restaurant first opened in Carroll Gardens in 2017 and quickly picked up a fervent following, who praised the restaurant’s intensely spicy dishes and its commitment to southern Thai dishes that were, at the time, less commonly found in the city. The popular and beloved restaurant closed in the final days of 2024, citing that chef Sirichai Sreparplarn was “tired and just needs a long break.” Sreparplarn is still behind the new version of Ugly Baby, which will have double the capacity of the original location and will feature a wider range of dishes. In Ugly Baby’s absence, some of its former employees went on to open Hungry Thirsty in the same location; it also welcomed a Manhattan sibling last month, the fiery Hungry Spicy. 364 Grand Street, between Havemeyer Street and Marcy Avenue

Update, 4:09 p.m.: This article, originally published at 10:55 a.m., has been updated to correctly reflect iDen’s Beijing Duck House’s reopening status.

items.text:
I love New York City in the summer, especially this past one, but I grew up in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains. I’m in my late 20s, I rock climb, and I live in Brooklyn, so of course I have an upstate New York itinerary for you. My partner’s mom’s partner (yes) has a cabin in Accord, New York, that we’ve been lucky to house sit, and I’ve fully fallen in love with the Catskills. Over the past few months, I’ve been so grateful to escape for a few long weekends among the trees and the birds and the slightly cooler weather of the Hudson Valley.

When I tell people in the city about my trips upstate, they’re often surprised to hear me gush about the restaurants. And while I think you could make all your meals (the bounty at the farm stands and markets make cooking very dreamy up there) and still have a great time, I can also strongly make the case for a dining-focused trip. Here’s where to go.

Day 1: Friday

If you’re heading up from the city, there are a few transit options (a bus from Port Authority to New Paltz or Kingston, the Metro North to Poughkeepsie, Amtrak to Hudson), but you’ll want a car to get around once you’re in the Catskills. I journey upstate via a car, which we pick up in New Jersey; that means that I get to grab Corner Slice’s massive, pillowy garlic knots as a pre-trip snack. If you find yourself in the area, I recommend you do the same.

Lunch

Stop at Storm King Art Center to take in the outdoor sculptures or catch a concert (I saw Dev Hynes’ ensemble there this summer and it was one of the most beautiful shows I’ve ever been to). I know museum restaurants are better than ever these days, but readers of this newsletter would probably appreciate that you can bring your own food and picnic, so I say pack a lunch. Anything goes; I’ve seen Panda Express from the nearest rest stop in those fields.

Dinner

Drive a little farther north and you’ll hit New Paltz, your first introduction to the charms of Upstate. Grab dinner at Shorties, a self-described “bar for the whole family” that lives up to the premise with DJs every night and pinball. A kimchi-topped hot dog is my move, but yours could be green pozole stew, togarashi-rubbed wings, or prosciutto- and pepperoncini-topped nachos. For those who are driving, a bonus at this spot is that the N/A drinks are good, with fun ingredients like salted guava juice. If you’re staying for longer than a night or two and planning to cook, stop by the fishmonger Gadaleto’s for all your seafood needs, while you’re in New Paltz. And if you’re planning to climb, you can rent pads from Rock & Snow.

Drinks

I stay in the Accord area, where lodging ranges wildly, from cabin Airbnbs to a souped-up retro motel to the luxury hotel Inness. The latter has a lovely (but pricey) restaurant for a group. Take in the same vibe (and view of the sunset) right outside the restaurant from the outdoor bar, where you can sit on Adirondack chairs around the fire and pretend you’re one of the celebrity guests. For a night-in alternative, grab a bottle of natural wine at Bluebird Wine Shop, which is next to the cutest grocery store, Accord Market — I like to stop in and pick up pie or ice cream for at-home (in-cabin?) dessert and drinks.

Day 2: Saturday

Lunch

In the morning, grab a coffee and pastry from Black Dot Cafe on your way to a hike at Minnewaska State Park, which has many trail options of varying lengths and levels of difficulty. Alternatively, if you’re a climber, go to the Mohonk Preserve. Both are beautiful, and — crucially for our purposes here — close to a really great German restaurant for lunch. The Mountain Brauhaus is a scene. I’ve never seen the family-owned German restaurant not packed with people, and as soon as you’re inside, you’ll see why. The portions are massive; the dirndl-clad servers are charming and personable; slices of pumpernickel come with most dishes, and I’ve witnessed people try and then subsequently order a loaf to take home — it’s that good. Recount your jaunt in nature over a wienerschnitzel, some spaetzle, a wheat beer with a slice of lemon, and excellent people watching.

A Snack and an Activity

Skate off the schnitzel at Skate Time, a retro roller rink run by the people behind Bjorn Qorn. You’re here to skate, yes, but also to have some pierogies from Helena’s Pierogis (the pierogi shop’s brick-and-mortar location in Kerhonkson is cash-only, so it’s a bonus to me, a serial non-cash-haver, that you can enjoy them here under the glow of popcorn-funded lights).

Dinner

Westwind Orchard is a staple for me. I was one of those people who didn’t really understand the hype of a good summer tomato until I had a life-changing panzanella here a few years ago. The ambiance here is the main attraction — parents let their children run free in the fields, there’s sometimes salsa dancing and live music, you’re surrounded by apple trees. Still, the food is better than it needs to be and so what you want when you’re on a trip where nature is the focus: fresh, seasonal, and simple. Get the aforementioned panzanella and don’t decide between pizza or pasta; get both. I like the pappardelle and the seasonal pizza is reliably excellent (right now, it’s summer squash and blossoms). Westwind is a cidery, but if you’re like me and not the biggest cider fan, rest assured that there are also classic cocktails highlighting New York ingredients, like a Negroni Sbagliato with cider as the bubbly topper.

Day 3: Sunday

Breakfast

Head north to Kingston. Have a cortado and a frittata from Village Coffee and Goods, then make your way around the town, which is one of my favorites in the area and a shopping destination for antiques, records, vintage clothing, and books.

Lunch

Rosie General is my favorite all-day cafe. I always get a mortadella sandwich or a chile-crisp-topped egg toast here. Recently, I surveyed the room and realized it seemed like every sandwich had its own dedicated kind of bread (some on English muffins, some on ciabatta, some on baguettes) made in-house; I really admire that level of commitment to detail. I generally prefer an edible souvenir to a trinket, and the shoppy shop-esque pantry of homemade mustards, pickles, infused oils and vinegars is a great place to pick one up.

Afternoon Pit Stops

Many NYC people travel upstate just to go to Stissing House; us included. On the way, we discovered Zabriskie’s Waterfall near the Bard College campus. It’s a swimming hole, but the vibe is more lean against a rock and read. When happy hour comes around, check out C. Cassis. You might associate cassis with old-timey France, but C. Cassis is doing it differently. Here, the blackcurrant liqueur isn’t sticky sweet, and you can enjoy it in fun applications like a piña colada, while learning more about the ingredient from friendly bartenders.

Dinner

Waiting for your table at Stissing House is actually part of the fun, because if you come sans reservation, you’re offered a seat and a drink in a living room-like space with candles and serve-yourself peanuts. I happily sipped a martini there, humming music from The Testament of Ann Lee (it’s very that vibe, honestly), awaiting a dinner of ham and pickles, fish pie, and steak. Skip dessert here (it’s fine, but I have a better plan). Back in the Accord area, hit Cherries Roadside; it’s classic Americana in a way that I have to say speaks to me. There is ice cream, sundaes, and milkshakes, but I always go with vanilla soft-serve — enjoy while marveling at the fact that you didn’t have to wait in one of the absurdly long froyo lines back in the city.

Honorable Mentions (and Where I Want to Hit Next Time

Harana Market makes some of my favorite Filipino food in the United States; they no longer have a dining room, but watch for pop-ups or takeaway opportunities (or if you have a big enough group, get catering!). Eng’s Chinese in Kingston is a slice of local history; I’ve so far only gotten (great) takeout, but I want to check out its dining room next. I recently had a head cheese sandwich from Cafe Mutton, in Hudson, that rocked my world. And if you are wine-inclined, Kingston Wine Co. sells some of the coolest bottles in the state, and Mirador, also in Kingston, is a great spot for sherry and pintxos. I’m also dying to check out the Oaxacan food scene in Poughkeepsie.

There are too many places to fit in one weekend, so I made you a list of more favorites in the Eater app. Follow me for more of my curated picks from the Northeast. (Subscribe to our travel newsletter, too!)

items.title: 不评判好坏，只鼓励创作：这款AI原生游戏，让人人都享受讲故事
items.summary: 文丨寒刃
items.text:
文丨寒刃 二几


到了2026年，AI叙事游戏仍然要面对一个灵魂拷问：在完全自由的文本创作中，玩家到底该怎么知道自己要讲什么？


6年前，在《千夜之书1001》还只有基于GPT-2的雏形demo时，制作人起司就在尝试回应这个问题。如今，经过数年的开发和迭代，《千夜之书1001》终于为玩家搭起了一套“脚手架”，帮助玩家享受讲故事的乐趣。


《千夜之书1001》是国内最早一批试水AI原生叙事玩法的项目。故事背景脱胎于经典文本《一千零一夜》，玩家扮演的山鲁佐德，在与妹妹的故事接龙中意外解锁将文字故事中的武器化作实体的能力。玩家需要持续为AI国王讲述故事，从而制造武器，最终杀死残暴的国王。

游戏steam商店页面

最终决斗画面


对于一款把“AI对话”本身变成玩法的游戏来说，“让玩家开口”只是第一步。玩家讲什么，AI如何理解，游戏如何回应玩家的创作，都是《千夜之书1001》接下来需要回答的问题。


人人都能从讲故事中获得快乐


《千夜之书1001》的早期DEMO称作《1001夜》，体验非常简洁：


玩家唯一需要做的事情就是给AI国王讲故事，在故事中自然讲出含有武器的内容，并最终用这些武器击败国王。在这个过程中，AI国王会基于自己的人设背景对故事做出反馈和引导，意图过于明显的故事可能惹怒国王，直接触发处决结局。

游戏早期画面

处决结局


对于本就擅长讲故事的玩家来说，游戏的乐趣显而易见：与AI国王斗智斗勇的同时，创作本身就是快乐的。讲出精彩或离谱的故事，也颇具成就感。


但如何让不擅长讲故事，或疲于创作的玩家，也能享受讲故事的乐趣？起司表示，要给玩家搭好“脚手架”。


首先，游戏需要让玩家知道怎么开始讲故事。早期DEMO只有一句话的提示，如今游戏加入了“灵感卡”系统，可以把进入寝殿前的经历直接当做故事的开头。另外多周目游玩的玩家，还可以选择“故事书”续写上一局没写完的故事。

灵感卡与故事书界面


游戏还加入一项“辅助名字”功能。起因是起司发现，如果玩家把自己认识的人或者熟悉的角色写进故事里，往往会有更好的节目效果，于是干脆顺着这个行为设计功能。在北京Dice Con展会现场，有多位玩家以“牛来”为主角创作，引得众人围观，视频在小红书获得近400点赞。

展会现场视频


有了顺畅的开头，游戏还需要让玩家知道自己的讲述正在产生什么影响。早期版本中，国王的情绪状态是半隐藏的，玩家往往要等到国王生气，才意识到自己的行为已经改变了他的状态。后续团队发现，游戏可以不给故事的文本打分，而给讲故事中的操作加分，比如激怒国王或哄国王开心，一句话里触发了多个道具等。这样明确的反馈可以帮助玩家理解游戏正在发生什么，从而更明确自己下一步行动。


起司表示，这一设计的目标并不是鼓励“好故事”，而是对所有“讲故事”的行为做出鼓励。种种设计都是让玩家觉得，讲故事本身是一件有趣、值得投入，而且能够得到回报的事情。


所以《千夜之书1001》也对于玩家的各种“骚操作”非常包容。比如把“刃”这样的字眼写进“辅助名字”里，就可以轻易让国王再次提到这个名字，并触发武器。

国王的故事中出现了寒刃的名字


在起司看来，这些行为并不一定需要被当成Bug修复。只要玩家能够想到一种方式，利用系统让故事产生意料之外的结果，这本身就是一种游戏行为，也是游戏乐趣的一部分。


从“讲故事”到“玩故事”


最早的《千夜之书1001》是起司在博士期间的研究项目，还发了论文。但随着项目越来越大，想承载的东西越来越多，它也逐渐从一个实验性Demo变成了一款完整的游戏。这意味着游戏需要有完整的剧情与世界观，让碎片化的即兴创作，落地为有温度、有记忆点、可长线沉淀的游戏内容。


起司认为，自己在开发过程中犯过最大的错误，就是低估了剧情的难度。单纯复刻《一千零一夜》的故事是远远不够的，起司希望女主成为一个“真实存在过的人”，有自己的生命历程。

山鲁佐德的童年故事


在创作期间的大量废案让起司真切体会到，为什么业内都说“游戏的第二关最难做”。团队最初为女主刺杀国王的行为设计的动因，是妹妹遭遇意外，但这样的设定，会让妹妹没有主体性。经过与编剧的反复磨合，团队最终引入咒印的核心设定，让女主的抗争与救赎更有支撑，整体故事逻辑也更加严密自洽。


补全世界观和人物背景后，起司认为，如今的《千夜之书1001》，很像一个叙事游戏。后续剧情还会出现园丁、医生、将军等形形色色的角色；女孩们手腕的咒印设定、山鲁佐德踏上救赎之路的初衷，所有伏笔与留白，都会在剧情中逐一揭晓。

在故事中，女孩们的手上会浮现出咒印。当咒印变红，她们就会成为国王的“新娘”。

山鲁佐德与想要成为将军的童年好友


团队是从游戏里生长出来的


《千夜之书1001》的另一个特别之处是，作为一款AI原生游戏，它是随着AI的发展一步步成型的，见证了这个快速迭代的AI时代。


最初的Demo可以追溯到6年前起司大学时期做的一次课题，当时GPT-2刚刚流行。《千夜之书1001》的开发团队正式组建并运作起来，其实只有一年多。

团队简介


从学术项目到上线Steam，《千夜之书1001》的商业化没有一个清晰的“转折时刻”。起司认为，这更像是一种渐进式的生长。随着大模型逐渐成熟，行业开始出现新的生态，团队自身也不断成长，而这个Demo本身又逐渐证明了自己“值得被继续做下去”。


由于没有同类参考作品，项目自始至终没有固定的发展方向，甚至难以界定游戏的类型。团队依靠玩家反馈，一点点调整优化内容。早期，Demo还在作为学术项目研发，团队曾经研究过实时场景生成等功能，来让玩家获得更强的沉浸感和反馈。但后来发现效果并不好，玩家接受度也不高，于是直接砍掉。起司认为，这类决策更多是在不断与玩家碰撞之后做出的。

被砍掉的实时场景生成功能


同样，这款游戏的制作团队，也不同于多数独立游戏工作室。起司形容团队是“随着游戏的完善慢慢生长出来的”，而不是走立项、拉投资、研发、发行的路子。


AI技术的发展，也改变了团队的工作流。现在团队的非技术人员，也可以通过vibe coding制作玩法demo，甚至直接完成一些小型功能的研发。队内也形成了“show me the demo”的工作方式，策划提出新需求时，会先做出demo给到程序，简化沟通和开发流程。


这也正是本作最特别的地方：游戏、团队、技术三者同步成长，构成了《千夜之书1001》项目的核心底色。AI原生游戏本就是个没有成熟参考、固定方向的全新赛道，项目更新、团队建设、技术迭代同步进行，彼此相互影响、共同成型。


聊起对AI行业的看法，起司表示，如果不是技术乐观者，大概也不会愿意深耕AI原生娱乐。她认为未来token成本会持续降低，AI技术也会持续进步，整条赛道还有很大的发展空间。在起司看来，当下各类AI原生游戏之间，比起竞争，更像是互相陪伴、共同成长。

blocks.x: 文丨寒刃 二几
到了2026年，AI叙事游戏仍然要面对一个灵魂拷问：在完全自由的文本创作中，玩家到底该怎么知道自己要讲什么？
6年前，在《千夜之书1001》还只有基于GPT-2的雏形demo时，制作人起司就在尝试回应这个问题。如今，经过数年的开发和迭代，《千夜之书1001》终于为玩家搭起了一套“脚手架”，帮助玩家享受讲故事的乐趣。
《千夜之书1001》是国内最早一批试水AI原生叙事玩法的项目。故事背景脱胎于经典文本《一千零一夜》，玩家扮演的山鲁佐德，在与妹妹的故事接龙中意外解锁将文字故事中的武器化作实体的能力。玩家需要持续为AI国王讲述故事，从而制造武器，最终杀死残暴的国王。
游戏steam商店页面
最终决斗画面
对于一款把“AI对话”本身变成玩法的游戏来说，“让玩家开口”只是第一步。玩家讲什么，AI如何理解，游戏如何回应玩家的创作，都是《千夜之书1001》接下来需要回答的问题。
人人都能从讲故事中获得快乐
《千夜之书1001》的早期DEMO称作《1001夜》，体验非常简洁：
玩家唯一需要做的事情就是给AI国王讲故事，在故事中自然讲出含有武器的内容，并最终用这些武器击败国王。在这个过程中，AI国王会基于自己的人设背景对故事做出反馈和引导，意图过于明显的故事可能惹怒国王，直接触发处决结局。
游戏早期画面
处决结局
对于本就擅长讲故事的玩家来说，游戏的乐趣显而易见：与AI国王斗智斗勇的同时，创作本身就是快乐的。讲出精彩或离谱的故事，也颇具成就感。
但如何让不擅长讲故事，或疲于创作的玩家，也能享受讲故事的乐趣？起司表示，要给玩家搭好“脚手架”。
首先，游戏需要让玩家知道怎么开始讲故事。早期DEMO只有一句话的提示，如今游戏加入了“灵感卡”系统，可以把进入寝殿前的经历直接当做故事的开头。另外多周目游玩的玩家，还可以选择“故事书”续写上一局没写完的故事。
灵感卡与故事书界面
游戏还加入一项“辅助名字”功能。起因是起司发现，如果玩家把自己认识的人或者熟悉的角色写进故事里，往往会有更好的节目效果，于是干脆顺着这个行为设计功能。在北京Dice Con展会现场，有多位玩家以“牛来”为主角创作，引得众人围观，视频在小红书获得近400点赞。
展会现场视频
有了顺畅的开头，游戏还需要让玩家知道自己的讲述正在产生什么影响。早期版本中，国王的情绪状态是半隐藏的，玩家往往要等到国王生气，才意识到自己的行为已经改变了他的状态。后续团队发现，游戏可以不给故事的文本打分，而给讲故事中的操作加分，比如激怒国王或哄国王开心，一句话里触发了多个道具等。这样明确的反馈可以帮助玩家理解游戏正在发生什么，从而更明确自己下一步行动。
起司表示，这一设计的目标并不是鼓励“好故事”，而是对所有“讲故事”的行为做出鼓励。种种设计都是让玩家觉得，讲故事本身是一件有趣、值得投入，而且能够得到回报的事情。
所以《千夜之书1001》也对于玩家的各种“骚操作”非常包容。比如把“刃”这样的字眼写进“辅助名字”里，就可以轻易让国王再次提到这个名字，并触发武器。
国王的故事中出现了寒刃的名字
在起司看来，这些行为并不一定需要被当成Bug修复。只要玩家能够想到一种方式，利用系统让故事产生意料之外的结果，这本身就是一种游戏行为，也是游戏乐趣的一部分。
从“讲故事”到“玩故事”
最早的《千夜之书1001》是起司在博士期间的研究项目，还发了论文。但随着项目越来越大，想承载的东西越来越多，它也逐渐从一个实验性Demo变成了一款完整的游戏。这意味着游戏需要有完整的剧情与世界观，让碎片化的即兴创作，落地为有温度、有记忆点、可长线沉淀的游戏内容。
起司认为，自己在开发过程中犯过最大的错误，就是低估了剧情的难度。单纯复刻《一千零一夜》的故事是远远不够的，起司希望女主成为一个“真实存在过的人”，有自己的生命历程。
山鲁佐德的童年故事
在创作期间的大量废案让起司真切体会到，为什么业内都说“游戏的第二关最难做”。团队最初为女主刺杀国王的行为设计的动因，是妹妹遭遇意外，但这样的设定，会让妹妹没有主体性。经过与编剧的反复磨合，团队最终引入咒印的核心设定，让女主的抗争与救赎更有支撑，整体故事逻辑也更加严密自洽。
补全世界观和人物背景后，起司认为，如今的《千夜之书1001》，很像一个叙事游戏。后续剧情还会出现园丁、医生、将军等形形色色的角色；女孩们手腕的咒印设定、山鲁佐德踏上救赎之路的初衷，所有伏笔与留白，都会在剧情中逐一揭晓。
在故事中，女孩们的手上会浮现出咒印。当咒印变红，她们就会成为国王的“新娘”。
山鲁佐德与想要成为将军的童年好友
团队是从游戏里生长出来的
《千夜之书1001》的另一个特别之处是，作为一款AI原生游戏，它是随着AI的发展一步步成型的，见证了这个快速迭代的AI时代。
最初的Demo可以追溯到6年前起司大学时期做的一次课题，当时GPT-2刚刚流行。《千夜之书1001》的开发团队正式组建并运作起来，其实只有一年多。
团队简介
从学术项目到上线Steam，《千夜之书1001》的商业化没有一个清晰的“转折时刻”。起司认为，这更像是一种渐进式的生长。随着大模型逐渐成熟，行业开始出现新的生态，团队自身也不断成长，而这个Demo本身又逐渐证明了自己“值得被继续做下去”。
由于没有同类参考作品，项目自始至终没有固定的发展方向，甚至难以界定游戏的类型。团队依靠玩家反馈，一点点调整优化内容。早期，Demo还在作为学术项目研发，团队曾经研究过实时场景生成等功能，来让玩家获得更强的沉浸感和反馈。但后来发现效果并不好，玩家接受度也不高，于是直接砍掉。起司认为，这类决策更多是在不断与玩家碰撞之后做出的。
被砍掉的实时场景生成功能
同样，这款游戏的制作团队，也不同于多数独立游戏工作室。起司形容团队是“随着游戏的完善慢慢生长出来的”，而不是走立项、拉投资、研发、发行的路子。
AI技术的发展，也改变了团队的工作流。现在团队的非技术人员，也可以通过vibe coding制作玩法demo，甚至直接完成一些小型功能的研发。队内也形成了“show me the demo”的工作方式，策划提出新需求时，会先做出demo给到程序，简化沟通和开发流程。
这也正是本作最特别的地方：游戏、团队、技术三者同步成长，构成了《千夜之书1001》项目的核心底色。AI原生游戏本就是个没有成熟参考、固定方向的全新赛道，项目更新、团队建设、技术迭代同步进行，彼此相互影响、共同成型。
聊起对AI行业的看法，起司表示，如果不是技术乐观者，大概也不会愿意深耕AI原生娱乐。她认为未来token成本会持续降低，AI技术也会持续进步，整条赛道还有很大的发展空间。在起司看来，当下各类AI原生游戏之间，比起竞争，更像是互相陪伴、共同成长。

items.title: This European-style ‘shopping village’ near NYC has designer deals, great restaurants, and 150+ boutiques
items.author: Corey Fuller
items.summary:
New York’s newest luxury-shopping destination does not look much like a mall.


There are no sprawling indoor corridors, no food-court trays, and no frantic
items.text:
New York’s newest luxury-shopping destination does not look much like a mall.


There are no sprawling indoor corridors, no food-court trays, and no frantic laps around a parking lot trying to find your car.


Instead, a set of dramatic gates opens onto landscaped pedestrian streets, polished shopfronts, cafés, and a collection of fashion labels that would normally send you downtown, across the Atlantic, or to a department-store floor in Midtown.


Belmont Park Village has quietly transformed a former parking area beside UBS Arena in Elmont into a European-style outlet village, with designer fashion, hospitality-minded service, and discounts of up to 65% off retail prices.


It’s the first North American destination from The Bicester Collection, the group behind luxury outlet villages outside cities including London, Paris, Milan, Barcelona, and Dublin.


The Bicester Collection’s New York debut is now a little over a year old, but it still feels surprisingly under the radar for a place this close to Manhattan.


Source / Belmont Park Village
A little bit of Europe, just beyond Queens


Belmont Park Village officially opened a few years ago in October 2024, planted beside the city’s eastern edge in Elmont, Long Island.


The setting is intentional: rather than recreating another enclosed retail complex, the village is built around walkable, open-air streets, planted landscaping, a town-square atmosphere, and car-free paths meant for lingering between shops.


The inspiration comes from a model that has spent decades working abroad.


The Bicester Collection began with Bicester Village outside London in 1995, then expanded the concept across Europe and China. In Elmont, it has brought that same model to North America for the first time: luxury and premium labels in an outdoor village setting, with previous-season collections and a stronger emphasis on the visit itself than the usual outlet sprint.


It is less “quick stop for a pair of sneakers” and more “accidentally spend three hours browsing, eating lunch, and trying on something you did not expect to find.”


Designer names, without the full-price panic


Shopping is the main event here, of course and it’s only continuing to grow.


Belmont Park Village is working toward more than 150 off-price boutiques at full occupancy, with brands offering previous collections, rare pieces, and select archival finds at discounts of up to 65% off.


The Hollywood Reporter’s guide to Belmont Park Village notes that the shopping village has leaned into one-of-a-kind and runway-adjacent pieces, not just basic outlet inventory — offering unique opportunities for local shoppers they wouldn’t find anywhere else.


Current and recently announced names include:

Valentino


Vivienne Westwood


Thom Browne


Missoni


Coach


Cavalli


Orlebar Brown


RAINS


The North Face


Levi’s


Canali


Gianvito Rossi


A.P.C.


Brunello Cucinelli


Kiton

Several brands even selected Belmont Park Village for their first-ever North American outlet location, including Vivienne Westwood, Thom Browne, Missoni, Orlebar Brown, and RAINS.


QNS reports that the Village’s mix includes luxury fashion alongside more familiar premium names, making it workable whether you are looking for a standout occasion piece or simply a much better deal on a seasonal staple.


One particularly unusual draw: the Missoni shop is home to the largest collection of discounted Missoni Home products in the United States, while the luxury fashion boutiques can stock prior runway pieces and hard-to-find accessories.


There are also plenty of red-carpet looks and previous-season offerings from labels to be found as well, from brands like Valentino and Cavalli.

There is a James Beard chef involved, too


This is not a place designed to force you to leave the moment your bags are full.


The Village’s dining options include Hundredfold, a French-American brasserie from James Beard Award-winning chef Timothy Hollingsworth.


Hollingsworth, whose résumé includes The French Laundry, brings a menu that plays with classic comfort food through a fine-dining lens, including French bread pizza, steak au poivre, martini flights, and fries cooked in beef tallow.


There is also Le Botaniste, the popular plant-based restaurant with Manhattan roots, as well as Pret A Manger for a quicker coffee-and-snack break.


The result is exactly the point: a shopping destination where lunch is not an afterthought and the walk between stores is part of the experience.

Concierge service, hands-free shopping & free parking


Belmont Park Village is trying to make the logistics feel notably less chaotic than a typical outlet trip.


Visitors can use complimentary concierge services, including hands-free shopping.


Purchases can be held while you continue browsing, then collected later or brought to your car. On New York Islanders game days, shoppers can also arrange to have bags delivered to UBS Arena for pickup after the game.


And perhaps the most shocking luxury in the metropolitan New York shopping universe: parking is free.


The Village is also right next to UBS Arena, home of the New York Islanders and a frequent concert venue, while the historic Belmont Park racetrack is undergoing its own major redevelopment nearby.


That means a shopping trip can easily turn into a full day or night out, especially when a big concert, hockey game, or event is already on your calendar!


Getting to Belmont Park Village


Belmont Park Village is at 2601 Hempstead Turnpike in Elmont, NY, roughly 19 miles east of Midtown Manhattan.


The easiest public-transit option is the Long Island Rail Road to Elmont-UBS Arena, followed by the free Village shuttle.


It’s also about 15 minutes from JFK Airport by car, making it a potential last-minute stop before or after a flight.


For more information about Belmont Park Village and to see its full list of stores, head here!
